Your strawberry frosting containing FD&C Red No. 3 must stop being manufactured with that color additive by January 15, 2027. On that date, 21 CFR 74.303 is removed and all existing certificates for FD&C Red No. 3 cease to be effective for use in food (90 FR 4628; 91 FR 50475). Regarding product already on shelves: The January 2025 order (90 FR 4628) states explicitly that '[w]hen FD&C Red No. 3 has been used in food or ingested drugs while its certificate is still effective, such food or ingested drugs will not be regarded as adulterated by reason of the use of such color additive.' This means frosting manufactured and containing FD&C Red No. 3 used before January 15, 2027 (i.e., while the certificate was still effective) is NOT rendered adulterated after that date. Product lawfully made before the effective date may remain on shelves and be sold. However, any food manufactured using FD&C Red No. 3 after January 15, 2027, will be considered adulterated because the color additive will be uncertified and its listing revoked (90 FR 4628, citing 21 CFR 80.32(h)).

response.answer:
Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, codified at 21 CFR 101.65(d)), a food that does not qualify for one of the automatic exemptions (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups, or water/tea/coffee) must meet two main criteria to bear the 'healthy' claim:

1. **Food Group Equivalent (FGE) requirement**: The food must contain a specified amount of at least one food group equivalent from the food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free or low-fat dairy, lean meat/seafood/eggs/beans/peas/lentils/nuts/seeds). The specific FGE amounts vary by product category (individual food, mixed product, main dish, or meal) as set forth in 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v) and the associated tables. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(2)–(3); 89 FR 106064)

2. **Nutrient-to-Limit (NTL) requirement**: The food must not exceed specified limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, expressed as a percentage of the Daily Value for those nutrients. These limits also vary by product category. (21 CFR 101.65(d)(3)(ii)–(v); 89 FR 106064; see also 90 FR 10592 at passage describing the rule as requiring 'FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients')

As summarized in the background section of 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.'

response.answer: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section defines the general nutritional claims paragraph covering labeling claims that are implied nutrient content claims because they suggest that a food may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices due to its nutrient content. The general framework for implied nutrient content claims (including 'healthy') is set out in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which defines an implied nutrient content claim as one that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices, where there is also implied or explicit information about the nutrition content of the food (e.g., "healthy")' (21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii) as revised by document 2024-29957, 89 FR 106064). The specific criteria a food must meet to bear the 'healthy' claim are found in 21 CFR 101.65(d). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published on December 27, 2024 (89 FR 106064, document 2024-29957), with an effective date of April 28, 2025 (as delayed by document 2025-03118), and a compliance date of February 25, 2028.

response.answer:
No, that was not a fair reading in mid-2025, and it is definitively incorrect now.

**What was true in mid-2025:** The January 2025 order revoking FD&C Red No. 3 (90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16, Doc. 2025-00830) was subject to an automatic administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) as of February 18, 2025, triggered by the filing of objections. During that stay, the effective dates of January 15, 2027 (food uses, removal of 21 CFR 74.303) and January 18, 2028 (ingested drugs, removal of 21 CFR 74.1303) were suspended but not cancelled or moved. The order itself was a final binding order, not a proposal. An administrative stay does not mean a rule 'might never take effect'—it means the agency must evaluate the objections before the rule can proceed. The stated effective dates remained on the books, albeit unconfirmed during the stay period.

Saying the removal was 'not final' mischaracterized the legal posture: the January 2025 order was a final order issued under section 721(d) of the FD&C Act (90 FR 4628). The stay was a statutory procedural consequence of objections being filed, not a sign of legal infirmity or uncertainty about finality.

**What is the position now:** FDA published a document on August 5, 2026 (91 FR 50475, Doc. 2026-15920) that overrules all objections, denies requests for a public hearing, lifts the administrative stay, and explicitly confirms the effective dates of January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028. The document states: 'we are ending the administrative stay of the January 2025 order, and under the January 2025 order we are repealing the listing for FD&C Red No. 3 in § 74.303 as a color additive in food and § 74.1303 as a color additive in ingested drugs effective January 15, 2027, and January 18, 2028, respectively' (91 FR 50475). This constitutes 'final action on the objections' under section 701(e)(2) of the FD&C Act.

The revocation is therefore fully confirmed and binding. After January 15, 2027, use of FD&C Red No. 3 in food will render such food adulterated (90 FR 4628). No compliance date is separately stated; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027 for food uses.

response.answer: Under 21 CFR 101.65(a)(2), a 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim must be made in accordance with the general requirements for nutrient content claims in § 101.13, with one specific carve-out: § 101.13(h) is excepted when the nutrient content claim is made in accordance with paragraph (d) of § 101.65. Section 101.13(h) is the disclosure requirement that would otherwise mandate a statement such as 'See nutrition information for ___ content' when a food exceeds specified levels of fat, saturated fat, cholesterol, or sodium. This disclosure requirement does not apply to foods bearing the 'healthy' claim under § 101.65(d). All other provisions of § 101.13 — including requirements on claim type size (§ 101.13(f)), the general prohibition on nutrient content claims unless made in accordance with applicable regulations (§ 101.13(b)), and other general principles — remain applicable to a 'healthy' claim.

response.answer: Yes, your shelf-stable lentil soup labeled 'healthy' is affected by the updated definition of the term 'healthy' under the final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27). Until that compliance date, you may continue to use the 'healthy' claim under the prior criteria, but by February 25, 2028, your product must meet the updated requirements of 21 CFR 101.65(d) or you must remove the 'healthy' claim from the label.

Your supplier is partially correct in a narrow technical sense but draws the wrong conclusion. The Red No. 3 order (Doc 2025-00830, 90 FR 4628, published 2025-01-16) indeed sets no explicit 'compliance date' — it states only effective dates. However, the absence of a compliance date does not mean there is no hard deadline. It means the deadline IS the effective date itself. Once the effective date arrives, 21 CFR 74.303 is removed from the Code of Federal Regulations, and FD&C Red No. 3 is no longer a listed color additive for food use. After that date, any food containing Red No. 3 is adulterated under 21 U.S.C. 721(a). The operative deadline for food use is January 15, 2027 (for ingested drugs, January 18, 2028). There is no separate grace period or sell-through allowance stated in the order.

Important caveat: The order was subject to an administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026 (per Doc 2026-15920). That stay has now ended (in_force_now: false), and the timeline facts confirm that the stated effective dates have NOT been superseded. Therefore, January 15, 2027 remains the operative deadline for food-use provisions, derived from the effective date.

In summary: your supplier is wrong that there is 'no hard deadline.' The deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027 for food uses. After that date, food containing FD&C Red No. 3 would be adulterated. You should plan to exhaust or dispose of coloured inventory before that date.

response.answer: Your compliance memo's recorded date of January 15, 2025 is incorrect. The Red No. 3 revocation order (Document No. 2025-00830) was published in the Federal Register on January 16, 2025, at 90 FR 4628. This is confirmed by both the order itself (90 FR 4628) and the subsequent order lifting the administrative stay (91 FR 50475, published August 5, 2026), which repeatedly references 'the order that published in the Federal Register of January 16, 2025 (90 FR 4628).' The date January 15, 2027 is the effective date for the food-use provisions, not the publication date.
